title: The Airliner Is Born
summary: The first airline passengers sat in cold, noisy little cabins and wore coats to keep warm. Step by step, engineers built shiny metal airliners like the DC-3, nurses became the first stewardesses, and flying boats hopped across the Pacific. New instruments let pilots fly through clouds, and sealed cabins let planes fly high above the storms.

sections.heading: Buying a Ticket to the Sky
paragraphs: Imagine it is a chilly morning in August 1919, and you are standing on a grassy field at Hounslow Heath, just west of London. A converted wartime biplane waits for you, its engine coughing into life. On 25 August 1919 a company called Aircraft Transport and Travel began a daily service from here to Le Bourget, near Paris. It is often called the world's first regular daily international airline service. On that first day, according to one account, the plane carried just a single passenger, plus some cargo.

A few weeks later, on 7 October 1919, a group of Dutch businessmen founded KLM, Royal Dutch Airlines, with a young former army pilot named Albert Plesman in charge. Its first flight, on 17 May 1920, flew from Croydon Airport near London to Amsterdam, piloted by Jerry Shaw. Many of the early airlines of 1919 disappeared within a year or two, merged into new companies or changed their names. KLM is the oldest airline still flying under its original name, more than a century later.

Flying in those first airliners was nothing like flying today. The cabins were small boxes, sometimes made of wood and fabric, with a few wicker chairs to save weight. There was no heating worth mentioning, so passengers wore heavy coats, gloves and sometimes blankets. The engines were so loud that people had to shout or pass notes, and some airlines handed out cotton wool for passengers' ears. Planes flew low, often only a few hundred metres up, where the air is bumpy, so many passengers were airsick. Pilots navigated by following roads, railway lines and rivers, and when fog rolled in they simply landed in a field and waited. A trip from London to Paris took about two and a half hours if all went well, which was still far faster than a train and a ferry.

It was also expensive. A ticket cost about as much as a working person earned in weeks, so early passengers were mostly wealthy business people, journalists and adventurers. And there was a deeper problem: most early airlines could not make money from passengers at all. They survived on government subsidies and on mail contracts, because a sack of letters paid far better than a nervous traveller. KLM, for example, became famous for its long route to the Dutch East Indies, now Indonesia, first flown experimentally in 1924, with regular service from 1929, carrying mail and a handful of passengers on a journey that took many days and dozens of stops.

To turn flying into a real business, airlines needed bigger, safer, more comfortable airplanes that could carry enough passengers to pay their own way. Over the next twenty years, engineers would build exactly that.

sections.heading: Tin Geese and Modern Shapes
paragraphs: In America, an unexpected company jumped into the airplane business: Ford, the maker of the Model T car. On 11 June 1926 the Ford Trimotor made its first flight. As its name suggests, it had three engines, one on the nose and one under each wing, so that it could keep flying if one failed. It was made of metal, with its body, wings and even its control surfaces covered in corrugated aluminium, which is aluminium pressed into ridges like a tin roof to make it stiffer. People nicknamed it the Tin Goose.

Later versions could carry 17 passengers. That might not sound like much, but it was a big step up, and the strong metal construction made passengers feel safer than in wood-and-fabric planes. Trimotors flew passengers and mail for several of the early American airlines, and in November 1929 one named Floyd Bennett carried the explorer Richard Byrd and his crew on the first flight over the South Pole. About 199 Trimotors were built before production ended in 1933. A few still fly today, giving rides at air shows.

Then, on 8 February 1933, a plane flew that looked like the future. The Boeing 247 had all the ideas that modern airliners would use. Its skin was smooth aluminium that carried part of the load itself, instead of just being a covering stretched over a frame; engineers call this semi-monocoque construction. Its single wing was a cantilever wing with no struts or wires outside, like Hugo Junkers had dreamed of. Its main wheels folded up into the engine housings after takeoff to reduce drag, though a little of each wheel still stuck out. It even had an autopilot and rubber de-icing boots on the wings that could crack off ice by inflating.

Boeing Air Transport, which later became United Air Lines, ordered the first 60, and one 247 crossed the United States from San Francisco to New York in about 19 and a half hours, a record at the time. But the 247 had two weaknesses. It carried only 10 passengers, and its main wing spar, the strong beam inside the wing, ran right through the cabin, so passengers had to step over it on their way down the aisle. Because Boeing was selling its first batch to its own sister airline, rival airlines could not get 247s quickly. One of those rivals, TWA, went to a different company in California with a challenge. That company was Douglas.

sections.heading: The DC-3: The Plane That Paid Its Own Way
paragraphs: Donald Douglas's team answered TWA with the DC-1, a single prototype flown in 1933, followed by the slightly bigger DC-2, which carried 14 passengers. Then came a famous long-distance telephone call. C. R. Smith, the head of American Airlines, wanted a plane with beds in it, so passengers could sleep on overnight flights across the country. Douglas agreed to build a wider, longer version of the DC-2 once American promised to buy 20 of them.

The result was the Douglas Sleeper Transport, which first flew on 17 December 1935, exactly 32 years after the Wright brothers' first flight at Kitty Hawk. The daytime version, with seats instead of berths, became the DC-3. American Airlines began passenger service on 26 June 1936. Its two radial engines, each giving about 1,000 to 1,200 horsepower, carried it along at about 330 km/h, and depending on the seating it could hold 21 to 32 passengers. It could fly from New York to Los Angeles with three stops, taking about 15 hours eastbound and about 17 and a half hours westbound, when the wind was against it.

Why was the DC-3 such a big deal? Because of simple arithmetic. Running an airplane costs money for fuel, pilots and repairs whether the seats are full or empty. The DC-3 carried enough passengers, flew fast enough and cost little enough to run that it was one of the first airliners able to make a profit from passengers alone, without needing mail money. Within a few years, the great majority of American airline passengers were flying on DC-3s, and airlines around the world, from KLM in Europe to companies in South America and Asia, bought them too.

When the Second World War came, the DC-3 put on a uniform. Its military versions, such as the C-47 Skytrain, known in Britain as the Dakota, carried troops, supplies, parachutists and wounded soldiers. The Soviet Union built its own version, the Lisunov Li-2, and Japan built one too. Altogether, counting civilian and military versions, more than 16,000 were built, and only about 600 of them were original civilian DC-3s.

Pilots loved the DC-3 for being tough and forgiving, and it lasted far longer than anyone expected. Some were still carrying passengers and cargo in remote places more than 85 years after the first one flew. A popular saying among pilots goes that the only replacement for a DC-3 is another DC-3.

sections.heading: Ellen Church and the First Stewardesses
paragraphs: Early airliners often had a co-pilot or a young cabin boy to help passengers, but in 1930 a young woman from Cresco, Iowa, had a new idea. Ellen Church was a registered nurse who had also learned to fly. She wanted to be an airline pilot, but airlines would not hire women to fly their planes. So she went to Steve Stimpson, a manager at Boeing Air Transport in San Francisco, with another suggestion. Many people were frightened of flying, she pointed out. Wouldn't they feel calmer if a trained nurse was on board to look after them?

Boeing Air Transport agreed to a three-month trial. Church became chief stewardess and recruited seven other nurses; together they are often remembered as the Original Eight. The rules were strict and show the attitudes of the time: stewardesses had to be single, under 25 years old, shorter than about 1.63 metres and lighter than about 52 kilograms, because space and weight on the planes were so precious. They earned 125 dollars a month.

On 15 May 1930, Ellen Church made her first flight as a stewardess, on a trip of about 20 hours from the San Francisco Bay Area to Chicago, with many stops along the way. Her job was much bigger than serving coffee and sandwiches. Stewardesses helped load luggage, sometimes helped with refuelling, wound the cabin clocks, swatted flies, comforted airsick passengers, and in an emergency used their nursing skills. Passengers liked the new service so much that other airlines quickly copied it.

Church's own flying career ended after about 18 months, when a car accident injured her. She went back to nursing and studied further at the University of Minnesota. During the Second World War she served as a flight nurse in the US Army Nurse Corps, caring for wounded soldiers on evacuation flights, and she was awarded the Air Medal. Today, the job she helped invent is called flight attendant and is done by women and men all over the world. Their most important role is still the one Church imagined: keeping passengers safe.

sections.heading: Clippers Across the Pacific
paragraphs: In the 1930s there was a big problem with crossing oceans: there were almost no long runways anywhere along the way. The solution was to land on water. Flying boats are airplanes whose bodies are shaped like the hull of a boat, so they can take off from and land on harbours, lagoons and calm bays. The American airline Pan American Airways, led by Juan Trippe, built a network of flying-boat routes and named its big planes Clippers, after the fast sailing ships of the 1800s.

The most daring route of all crossed the Pacific Ocean, the largest ocean on Earth. Pan Am built bases on a chain of islands like stepping stones: Hawaii, the tiny atolls of Midway and Wake, and Guam. On Wake Island there was nothing at all, so the company shipped in workers and equipment, and by some accounts even soil and plants, to build a hotel and a radio station.

On 22 November 1935, the Martin M-130 flying boat China Clipper took off from Alameda, on San Francisco Bay, carrying about 111,000 letters. Up to 100,000 people are estimated to have watched from the shores of the bay. The captain was Edwin Musick, and the navigator was Fred Noonan, the same man who would vanish with Amelia Earhart less than two years later. Hopping from Honolulu to Midway, Wake and Guam, the China Clipper reached Manila, in the Philippines, on 29 November, after a total flying time of about 59 hours and 48 minutes. A voyage that took weeks by ship had shrunk to less than a week.

Paying passengers followed in October 1936. Later, in 1939, Pan Am's even bigger Boeing 314 flying boats began crossing the Atlantic. The 314 was like a flying ocean liner: it could carry 68 passengers by day or 36 in sleeping berths at night, and its lounge turned into a dining room in the evening, with tablecloths and waiters serving full meals. In January 1943, President Franklin D. Roosevelt flew in one to a wartime conference in Casablanca, making the Boeing 314 the first airplane to carry a sitting American president.

Flying boats were glamorous, but their days were numbered. They were slow and expensive to run, and during the Second World War so many long runways were built around the world that land planes could go almost anywhere. By the late 1940s the great Clippers had all been retired.

sections.heading: Flying Blind: Instruments and Radio Beams
paragraphs: For the first 25 years of flying, a pilot's most important instrument was the window. Pilots kept the plane level by watching the horizon, and found their way by spotting landmarks. Fog and cloud were deadly. Inside a cloud, with no horizon to see, your inner ear, the balance organ inside your head, can easily be fooled. A pilot can be in a slowly tightening turn, or even diving, while feeling completely sure that the plane is flying straight and level. Many early crashes happened exactly this way.

To solve this, the Daniel Guggenheim Fund for the Promotion of Aeronautics, set up in 1926 by the businessman Daniel Guggenheim and his son Harry, paid for research into what it called fog flying. Its star pilot was Lieutenant Jimmy Doolittle of the US Army, who was not only a daring racing pilot but also held a doctorate in aeronautics from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, one of the first such degrees in the United States.

Doolittle and his team gathered three new instruments. The first was an artificial horizon, made by the Sperry company, using a fast-spinning gyroscope that stays pointing the same way in space; a little picture of a plane in front of a horizon line showed the pilot whether his wings were level and his nose up or down. The second was a directional gyro, another gyroscope that showed which way the plane was heading far more steadily than a wobbly magnetic compass. The third was a new, very sensitive altimeter invented by Paul Kollsman, which measured air pressure so precisely that it could show the plane's height to within about 3 metres. On top of that, radio beacons on the ground sent out signals that a needle in the cockpit could follow toward the airfield.

On 24 September 1929, at Mitchel Field on Long Island, New York, Doolittle climbed into the rear cockpit of a Consolidated NY-2 biplane, and a canvas hood was pulled over him so that he could see nothing outside. In the front cockpit sat a safety pilot, Lieutenant Ben Kelsey, ready to take over if something went wrong, who held his hands up outside the cockpit so that observers could see he was not touching the controls. Doolittle took off, flew a course of about 15 minutes, turned, came back and landed, all without ever seeing the ground. It was the first time a pilot had taken off, flown and landed using instruments alone.

Through the 1930s, a system called the radio range spread across America. Ground stations sent out the Morse code letter A, dot-dash, in some directions and N, dash-dot, in others. Where the two signals overlapped, they merged into one steady hum in the pilot's headphones. Flying along that steady tone was like walking along an invisible fence; if you drifted off, you heard the dots and dashes of A or N and knew which way to turn. Together with gyroscopic instruments, radio navigation let airlines keep their schedules even when the weather was poor, which made flying far more reliable and safer.

sections.heading: Above the Weather: The Pressurized Cabin
paragraphs: Even with good instruments, most airliners of the 1930s had to fly through the weather, not over it. Storms, ice and bumpy clouds usually lie in the lower few kilometres of the sky. Higher up, the air is smoother and thinner, and thinner air also means less drag, so a plane can fly faster on the same fuel. But there is a catch: at around 6,000 metres the air has only about half as much oxygen in each breath as at sea level. Without help, passengers would become dizzy, confused and eventually unconscious.

The answer was to seal the cabin and pump extra air into it, like blowing up a balloon, so that the air inside stays thicker than the air outside. This is called a pressurized cabin. The first airliner to carry passengers this way was the Boeing 307 Stratoliner, which first flew on 31 December 1938. It used the wings and tail of Boeing's B-17 bomber attached to a new, round body, because a round tube is the best shape for holding air pressure, just as soda cans and submarines are round.

Pan American started flying the Stratoliner on 4 July 1940, followed by TWA a few days later. It carried 33 passengers in comfort and cruised at about 350 km/h at heights of up to about 6,000 metres. While it flew that high, the cabin was kept at a pressure similar to being on a mountain about 3,700 metres high; at slightly lower cruising heights the cabin felt more like 2,400 metres, which is about the cabin altitude of modern airliners today. Passengers could sit back while storms rumbled far below them.

Why not keep the cabin at full sea-level pressure? Because the difference between the air pressure inside and the thinner air outside pushes outward on every part of the cabin walls, windows and doors. The bigger that difference, the stronger and heavier the body must be, and every extra kilogram of metal means fewer passengers or less fuel. So engineers choose a compromise: air thick enough to breathe comfortably, but not so thick that the plane has to be built like a submarine. You can feel this compromise yourself on any flight today. As the plane climbs and the cabin pressure slowly drops, the air trapped inside your middle ear pushes outward, and your ears pop when it escapes through a small tube to the back of your throat. Swallowing or yawning helps that tube open, which is why people chew gum or give babies a drink during takeoff and landing.

The Stratoliner's story also shows the cost of progress. One of the prototypes crashed during a test flight in March 1939, killing all ten people on board. Only ten Stratoliners were built, because the Second World War soon took over Boeing's factories. Yet the idea was here to stay. One restored Stratoliner, once Pan Am's Clipper Flying Cloud, survives today in the Smithsonian's collection.

sections.heading: World War II Reshapes the Sky
paragraphs: The Second World War, from 1939 to 1945, was the most destructive war in history, and once again airplanes changed faster than ever before. As with the First World War, it is worth remembering the terrible human cost behind the technology, including cities bombed from the air. But several wartime developments later made peacetime flying safer and more practical for everyone.

The first was radar, a way of finding objects by sending out radio waves and catching their echoes. Britain had built a chain of radar stations along its coast before the war. Then, in 1940, John Randall and Harry Boot at the University of Birmingham built a device called the cavity magnetron, which produced powerful, very short radio waves. Short waves made radar sets small enough to fit inside airplanes and sharp enough to see much smaller objects. Later that year British scientists carried a magnetron to the United States on a secret mission, and American laboratories began producing radar on a huge scale. After the war, radar became the basis of air traffic control, letting controllers on the ground track airliners through cloud and darkness. The same magnetron, by the way, is the part that heats your food in a microwave oven.

The second was the big four-engine airplane. Wartime bombers and transports, such as the B-17, the B-29 and the Douglas C-54, which was the military version of the four-engine DC-4, flew long distances across oceans every day. Their engines grew more powerful and dependable, and the B-29 even had pressurized crew areas. Lockheed's sleek, pressurized Constellation first flew in January 1943 and served as a military transport; after the war, TWA began flying Constellations across the Atlantic in February 1946.

The third was runways. Armies and air forces built thousands of long, hard concrete runways all over the world, from Pacific islands to Africa and the North Atlantic. Many later became civilian airports. London's Heathrow, for example, began as a wartime airfield taken over by the government in 1944. When it opened to civilian flights in 1946, its first passenger terminal was a row of army tents with wooden boards laid across the mud.

The war also left behind thousands of trained pilots, navigators and mechanics, and thousands of surplus transport planes that new airlines could buy cheaply. By the end of the 1940s, ordinary people were starting to fly in pressurized four-engine airliners like the Constellation and the Douglas DC-6, high above the weather, guided by radio and radar.

Yet there was a limit hiding in the propellers themselves. As propeller tips spin faster and faster, they approach the speed of sound, and they start losing efficiency and making shock waves. Propeller airliners topped out at cruising speeds of roughly 500 to 600 km/h, and no amount of extra engine power could push them much faster. To go faster, airplanes would need a completely new kind of engine. In fact, two young engineers, one in Britain and one in Germany, had already had a radical idea about how to build it.

deepDive: Economic historians often argue that the airliner was born twice: first as a technical possibility around 1919, and then as a business in the mid-1930s. Early airlines in Europe lived on government subsidies, and in the United States they lived on air mail contracts; passengers were almost a side business. The turning point came from a cluster of technologies arriving together in the early 1930s: stressed-skin aluminium structures, cantilever wings, retractable landing gear, wing flaps, controllable-pitch propellers and powerful, reliable air-cooled radial engines. The Boeing 247 of 1933 combined many of these, but with only 10 seats its seat-mile costs, the cost of carrying one passenger one mile, were too high. The DC-3 of 1935 added roughly two to three times the seating for only modestly higher operating costs, and that is why it is usually described as the first airliner that could make money carrying passengers alone. Its huge production run of over 16,000, almost all military, then flooded the post-war market with cheap, rugged transports. Safety and reliability required a second cluster of inventions. Doolittle's 1929 hooded flight showed that a pilot trained to trust gyroscopic instruments and a precise altimeter could fly without seeing the ground, and the radio range gave airlines invisible highways to follow. Pressurization, first offered to passengers in the Boeing 307 in 1940, let airliners cruise above much of the weather, but it introduced a new engineering challenge: every flight inflates and deflates the fuselage like a balloon, and those repeated stresses, called fatigue, would become a deadly problem in the jet age. Finally, the Second World War acted like a giant accelerator. It produced microwave radar thanks to the cavity magnetron, a global network of long concrete runways, four-engine long-range transports such as the C-54 and Constellation, and a huge pool of trained aircrew. Historians still debate how much the war sped up civil aviation compared with what peacetime research would have achieved, but the post-war airline boom clearly drew on all of these wartime legacies.
funFact: The DC-3's prototype first flew on 17 December 1935, exactly 32 years to the day after the Wright brothers' first flight.

check.q: What did Jimmy Doolittle prove with his flight on 24 September 1929?
check.a: That a pilot could take off, fly and land using instruments alone, without seeing outside.
wrong: That an airplane could cross the Pacific Ocean without stopping.
That a jet engine could power an airliner.
That passengers could sleep in beds on an airplane.
